## Deuteronomy 17 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overview of the Chapter

The chapter falls into three sections: (1) pure worship and the punishment of idolatry (vv. 1–7), (2) a higher court of appeal for difficult cases (vv. 8–13), and (3) laws governing Israel's future king (vv. 14–20). Ellicott notes that the unifying theme is "the supremacy in Israel of the written law of God" — truth, justice, and purity are demanded of all who draw near to Him (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-17.html).

---

### v. 1 — Unblemished Sacrifices

**"You shall not sacrifice to the LORD your God an ox or a sheep with any defect or serious flaw, for that is detestable to the LORD your God."**

- **Traditional reading (Guzik, Enduring Word):** God refused any sacrifice with a blemish, calling it "detestable" (*toebah*, an abomination). The principle is that God will not receive what costs us nothing. David Guzik notes King David illustrated this when he refused to offer burnt offerings "with that which costs me nothing" (2 Samuel 24:24) (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-17/).

- **Ellicott:** The law concerning purity of victims is given in full in Leviticus 22:17–25. The same principle unites the topics in this part of Deuteronomy — the holiness of the God of Israel demands truth, justice, and purity in all who approach Him. The only time in Israel's history when sacrificing imperfect creatures is notably complained of is Malachi's time (Malachi 1:7–14) (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-17.html).

- **Precept Austin:** The Hebrew for "defect" is literally "evil word" (*dabar ra*), meaning an "evil thing." Offering less than the best to God holds His majestic name in low esteem. The Septuagint renders "blemish" as *momos* and "defect" as *rhema poneros*. The word *toebah* (detestable/abomination) is a key Deuteronomy word occurring 16 times in the book (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-17-commentary).

- **Haydock (Catholic):** Briefly notes that any blemish or fault makes the sacrifice "an abomination" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/deuteronomy-17.html).

---

### vv. 2–3 — Idolatry as Covenant Transgression

**"If a man or woman among you … is found doing evil … by transgressing His covenant and going to worship other gods … the sun or moon or any of the host of heaven — which I have not commanded…"**

- **Gill:** These verses describe anyone guilty of idolatry in any of its forms — serving and worshipping other gods, including the celestial bodies. The phrase "which I have not commanded" means God never gave any command to worship such things; rather, He strictly forbade it (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/17.htm).

- **Precept Austin:** "Transgressing" is literally "passing over" (*abar*) — crossing the line of God's covenant. Idolatry is framed as high treason against the covenant. The mention of sun, moon, and stars recalls the Asherah and sacred pillars just mentioned in Deuteronomy 16:21–22 (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-17-commentary).

- **Ellicott:** Sun, moon, and stars represent "the oldest and simplest, and apparently most innocent form of idolatry." If even this was punishable by death, no grosser form could be spared. The Book of Job acknowledges this as a denial of "the God that is above" (Job 31:26–28). This section differs from Deuteronomy 13: there the penalty targets false prophets who led others astray; here it is directed at every individual idolater (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-17.html).

---

### vv. 4–5 — Thorough Investigation and Execution

**"…you must investigate it thoroughly. If the report is true and such an abomination has happened in Israel, you must bring out to your gates the man or woman … and you must stone that person to death."**

- **Guzik:** The judges were commanded to "inquire diligently." Investigation had to be thorough before any execution. The execution was to take place at the city gates — a public place — so the community would know the justice of what was being done (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-17/).

- **Gill:** The offender was to be brought forth only after being tried before a court of judicature, found guilty, and sentenced. The gates were the place of judgment and public execution (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/17.htm).

- **Ellicott:** Traces of this law appear in the covenant made under King Asa: "whosoever would not seek the LORD God of Israel should be put to death, whether small or great, whether man or woman" (2 Chronicles 15:13) (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-17.html).

---

### v. 6 — The Two-or-Three-Witness Standard

**"On the testimony of two or three witnesses a man shall be put to death, but he shall not be executed on the testimony of a lone witness."**

- **Guzik:** This high standard of evidence protected the innocent from false or secret accusations. It guaranteed the accused could face and cross-examine accusers. The standard of "two or three witnesses" is not necessarily only individuals — strong tangible evidence could also serve as a "witness." The same standard is applied in the New Testament to accusations against elders (1 Timothy 5:19) (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-17/).

- **Gill:** The testimony must be verbal, not written — it must come "at the mouth" of the witnesses. Rabbi Aben Ezra notes that if two witnesses contradict two others, a third turns the scale. Two qualified (wise) men suffice, or three of ordinary status (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/17.htm).

- **Precept Austin:** This is a safeguard requirement already established in Numbers 35:29–30. The requirement of multiple witnesses was a remarkably high bar for ancient Near Eastern justice (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-17-commentary).

---

### v. 7 — Witnesses Initiate the Execution

**"The hands of the witnesses shall be the first in putting him to death, and after that, the hands of all the people. So you must purge the evil from among you."**

- **Guzik:** The witnesses had to be so certain of what they saw that they were willing to cast the first stone. This made false testimony far less likely. The execution was a community event, supported by all the people. The phrase "purge the evil from among you" appears nine times in Deuteronomy and is quoted by Paul in 1 Corinthians 5:13 regarding church discipline (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-17/).

- **Ellicott:** "The hands of the witnesses … first" is "a great safeguard against false testimony." The Hebrew verb for "put away" (or "purge") literally means "consume" or "burn" — its primary meaning relates to burning. The Septuagint renders "the evil" as "the wicked man," which is the form Paul picks up in 1 Corinthians 5:13. Ellicott adds that this has bearing on the phrase "deliver us from evil" in the Lord's Prayer — there is no such thing as wickedness apart from some wicked person (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-17.html).

- **Guzik also notes:** This puts Jesus' words in John 8:7 ("He who is without sin among you, let him throw a stone at her first") in perspective: Jesus asked for the official witness to step forward and identify himself on record (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-17/).

---

### vv. 8–9 — The Higher Court of Appeal

**"If a case is too difficult for you to judge … you must go up to the place the LORD your God will choose. You are to go to the Levitical priests and to the judge who presides at that time."**

- **Guzik:** God provided courts of appeal — higher courts beyond local judges, consisting of priests and Levites who had greater knowledge of God's word. The Hebrew verb "too hard" (*pala*) is related to the word for "wonderful" or "miraculous," suggesting cases with very unusual features (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-17/).

- **Gill:** This points to Jerusalem and the great Sanhedrin, the supreme court to which inferior judges applied in matters of difficulty. "Between blood and blood" refers to cases of homicide where degrees of guilt had to be distinguished (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/17.htm).

- **Ellicott:** "Blood" and "plea" likely indicate criminal and civil cases respectively. "Stroke" (*nega*, the common word for "plague") may refer to cases of ceremonial purity or impurity, especially disease. An allusion to this law appears in Jehoshaphat's judicial reform (2 Chronicles 19:8–10). The priests are custodians of the Law; the judge is the executor of it. This order — priest first, then judge — matches the constitution Moses left behind (Numbers 27:15–21, where Joshua stands before Eleazar) (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-17.html).

- **Haydock (Catholic):** The "judge" here, according to the Rabbis and most commentators (Josephus, Philo, etc.), is the high priest, who abode near the tabernacle and could explain the law when arrayed with Urim and Thummim. Haydock notes that "some moderns, with Calvin, Ainsworth, etc., pretend that an appeal was to be made to the priests in religious disputes and to the civil magistrate in other cases," but insists the high priest was the final authority — the government was a theocracy and the pontiff acted as God's vicegerent (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/deuteronomy-17.html).

---

### vv. 10–11 — Binding Authority of the Higher Court

**"You must abide by the verdict they give you … Do not turn aside to the right or to the left from the decision they declare to you."**

- **Ellicott:** This is a crucial passage about the relationship between the Church (the priests) and the written Word. The function of the priest and judge was to "show, inform, teach, and tell" the sentence *of the law* — i.e., of the written law. They did not invent verdicts; they applied the law to cases. "The only authority wherewith the Church (of Israel, or of Christ) can 'bind' or 'loose' is the written Law of God." Our Lord's words in Matthew 23:2–3 about the Scribes and Pharisees sitting "in Moses' seat" apply this same principle: hear them insofar as they teach the law. The Rabbis acknowledged this by their constant appeal to Scripture (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-17.html).

- **Guzik:** The decision of the higher court was binding. To "not turn aside to the right or to the left" meant total compliance — no selective obedience (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-17/).

---

### vv. 12–13 — The Presumptuous Man and the Deterrent Effect

**"But the man who acts presumptuously, refusing to listen either to the priest … or to the judge, must be put to death. … Then all the people will hear and be afraid, and will no longer behave arrogantly."**

- **Ellicott:** The word "presumptuously" (*zadon*, related to pride) occurs for the first time here in Scripture. It denotes proud self-assertion against the law. In a theocracy, rebellion against God's law is treason, and death is the expected penalty. Once the law of Jehovah is separated from the law of the land, this changes — yet Ezra's commission from Artaxerxes (Ezra 7:25–26) permitted identifying God's law with Persian law to the full extent of this precept (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-17.html).

- **Guzik:** Treating God's appointed court with contempt was a capital crime. God thought it essential that courts and judges be respected in Israel. The public execution served as a deterrent: "all the people will hear and fear." This was not purely punitive but also preventative (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-17/).

---

### vv. 14–15 — The Future King: God's Choice, an Israelite Brother

**"When you enter the land … and you say, 'Let us set a king over us like all the nations around us,' you are to appoint over yourselves the king whom the LORD your God shall choose. Appoint a king from among your brothers; you are not to set over yourselves a foreigner…"**

- **Guzik:** God looked forward some 400 years to Israel's demand for a king. This was not a command to appoint a king, but permission with restrictions. God wanted the king to be of *His* choosing and at *His* timing. Saul exemplifies a king chosen by the nation at their timing; David exemplifies a king chosen by God at His timing. Though kingship was foreseen as early as the patriarchal promises (Genesis 17:6, 17:16, 35:11, 49:10), Israel had no king for over 500 years of its history (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-17/).

- **Gill:** The Jews traditionally took this as a command, but Gill argues it is only a permission in case they should desire a king, as God foresaw they would. The restriction that the king must be "from among your brethren" excluded even an Edomite (though called "brother" elsewhere) — pointing to Herod, an Idumean set up by the Romans, not by Israel. In this the king typified the Messiah: "their nobles shall be of themselves" (Jeremiah 30:21) (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/17.htm).

- **Pulpit Commentary:** The prohibition to choose a foreigner indicates the people had the right of election. How this was subject to the Divine choice is not spelled out. Judging from subsequent history, only on special occasions (the first king or a change of dynasty) did God take the initiative through a prophet; ultimately the monarchy became hereditary, with the prince understood to succeed with Divine approval unless God expressly intimated otherwise (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/17-15.htm).

- **Dummelow:** The people are not commanded to appoint a king (unlike the judges in Deuteronomy 16:18). The desire for a king is anticipated but not disapproved. The kingdom is theocratic — the king is God's vicegerent. Church and State are identical (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/deuteronomy-17.html).

- **Ligonier (Reformed):** Deuteronomy 17:14–20 ranks among the most influential biblical passages in history. It is one of the foundations for the traditional Western constitutional concept of *lex rex* — "the law is king" — meaning rulers are subject to the laws no less than ordinary citizens. Jesus is the true Son of David who keeps God's law perfectly and thereby earned the right to rule forever (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/king-and-law).

---

### v. 16 — The King Must Not Multiply Horses or Return to Egypt

**"But the king must not acquire many horses for himself or send the people back to Egypt to acquire more horses, for the LORD has said, 'You are never to go back that way again.'"**

- **Guzik:** The future king must not put undue trust in military might. Horses were the mighty weapons of the era when most soldiers fought on foot. Adam Clarke adds: "Lest the people might depend on a well-appointed cavalry as a means of security, and so cease from trusting in the strength and protection of God." The prohibition against returning to Egypt was both literal and symbolic — Egypt represented the life of bondage from which God had delivered them (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-17/).

- **Gill:** Multiplying horses was forbidden so the king would not trust in outward military strength rather than in God. The specific mention of Egypt recalls that Egypt was famous for its horses and chariots (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/17.htm).

- **Ellicott:** The caution against multiplying horses "marks the profound wisdom of the writer." Israel's strength was its infantry; most of Canaan's battlefields were unsuited for chariots and cavalry. An infantry army can choose its own ground (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-17.html).

- **Knox Translation (Catholic, via New Advent):** Rendered as: "he must not raise troop after troop of horsemen, and turn his people's eyes back towards Egypt, flushed with the pride of horsemanship." The footnote explains that what is discouraged is probably not an invasion of Egypt but securing an alliance with Egypt to obtain cavalry (https://www.newadvent.org/bible/deu017.htm).

---

### v. 17 — The King Must Not Multiply Wives or Wealth

**"He must not take many wives for himself, lest his heart go astray. He must not accumulate for himself large amounts of silver and gold."**

- **Guzik:** Three areas are covered: military power (horses), personal pleasure (wives), and wealth (silver and gold). Each was a matter of balance — the king had to have some but not "multiply." Solomon notoriously violated all three: 40,000 horse stalls (1 Kings 4:26), 700 wives and 300 concubines (1 Kings 11:3), and wealth surpassing all kings (1 Kings 10:23). Guzik notes that Solomon likely deceived himself by asking, "How much is 'multiply'? This isn't an exact number." The human heart has an astounding ability for self-deception. These three areas remain the places where many modern Christian leaders fall: power, pleasure, or money (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-17/).

- **Clarke:** "Neither shall he multiply wives — For this would necessarily lead to foreign alliances, and be the means of introducing the manners and customs of other nations, and their idolatry also. Solomon sinned against this precept, and brought ruin on himself and on the land by it" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/deuteronomy-17.html).

- **DesiringGod (Baptist/Reformed):** In an article on why God allowed polygamy in the Old Testament, notes that Deuteronomy 17:17 forbids Israel's future king from multiplying wives. The king was to be the ideal Israelite and a new Adam figure (cf. Psalm 8). This restriction shows that polygamy, though tolerated in the broader culture, was never God's ideal, especially for leaders (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/why-did-god-allow-polygamy).

---

### vv. 18–19 — The King Must Write and Read God's Law Daily

**"When he is seated on his royal throne, he must write for himself a copy of this instruction on a scroll in the presence of the Levitical priests. It is to remain with him, and he is to read from it all the days of his life, so that he may learn to fear the LORD his God…"**

- **Guzik:** It is striking to picture the king of Israel laboring over parchment with a pen, making a personal copy of the law. God wanted every king to also be a scribe. The copy was to be made from the official version kept by the priests, presumably near the ark (cf. Deuteronomy 31:9, 25–26). The king was to read it "all the days of his life" — daily meditation. F.B. Meyer is quoted: "The corrective suggested here is meditation on the Word of God … this would keep him in the lowlands of humility." John Trapp praised Queen Elizabeth I, who at her coronation received the Bible with both hands, kissed it, and said it had ever been her chief delight and would be the rule of her government (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-17/).

- **Gill:** The king's copy was to be with him always — at home or abroad, on the throne or lying down. The Jews observed exceptions for places where it was improper to read it (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/17.htm).

- **Pulpit Commentary:** He shall write it "with his own hand, say the Jews. Out of that which is before the priests — Out of that original, which was carefully kept by the priests in the sanctuary, that it might be a perfect copy, and that it might have the greater influence upon him, coming to him as from the hand and presence of God" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/deuteronomy/17-18.htm).

- **Ellicott:** The phrase "a copy of this law" (*mishneh hattorah hazot*) is the source of the Greek title *Deuteronomion* (hence "Deuteronomy"). The Septuagint mistranslated this as "this second law" (*to deuteronomion touto*), giving rise to the English name of the book. Ellicott notes traces of this direction in the coronation of Joash (2 Chronicles 23:11, "they gave him the testimony"), Jehoshaphat's teaching campaign (2 Chronicles 17:9), and Josiah's response to the discovered book (2 Chronicles 34:18). It is striking that we do not hear of the Book of the Law in connection with David and Solomon — possibly because David was himself a prophet (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-17.html).

- **Dummelow:** "A copy of this law" means not merely vv. 14–20 but the entire Deuteronomic law in the custody of the priests. At the coronation of Joash the "testimony" was put into his hands (2 Chronicles 23:11). Dummelow notes that to this day, when a Christian monarch is crowned, the Bible is delivered with the words: "We present you with this book, the most valuable thing that the world affords. Here is wisdom; this is the royal law" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/deuteronomy-17.html).

- **Catholic Encyclopedia (newadvent.org):** The term "Deuteronomy" occurs in Deuteronomy 17:18 and Joshua 8:32. It renders the Hebrew *mishneh*, signifying "copy" or "duplicate" rather than "repetition." The text itself demands this meaning: "he shall copy out to himself the Deuteronomy of this law in a volume, taking the copy of the priests of the Levitical tribe" (https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/04761b.htm).

---

### v. 20 — The Purpose: Humility, Obedience, and a Lasting Dynasty

**"Then his heart will not be exalted above his countrymen, and he will not turn aside from the commandment … in order that he and his sons may reign many years over his kingdom in Israel."**

- **Guzik:** Staying in God's word would keep the king properly humble. Matthew Poole is quoted: "The Scriptures, diligently read and studied, are a powerful and probable means to keep him humble, because they show him that, though a king, he is subject to a higher Monarch, to whom he must give an account … sufficient to abate the pride of the haughtiest person in the world." Adam Clarke (18th–19th c. Methodist) noted that the phrase "he and his sons" implies the crown was designed to be hereditary, which he judged "on the whole, the safest, and best calculated to secure the public tranquillity" (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-17/).

- **Ellicott:** The phrase "he and his children" shows the kingdom would be hereditary only so far as Jehovah willed. It is striking that no dynasty except David's ever continued more than five generations, and only two dynasties lasted more than two generations, while David's dynasty was perpetual by promise — a fact "could hardly have escaped notice, if known to the writer of this book" (an argument Ellicott uses for Mosaic authorship) (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-17.html).

- **Church Pulpit Commentary:** The true leader realises that as brother of those he rules, he must be sympathetic, accessible, generous-hearted, and patient. "In all these respects how high an example is set by the Divine Leader!" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cpc/deuteronomy-17.html).

---

### Points Where Protestant Traditions Differ

- **The identity of "the judge" in v. 9:** Haydock's Catholic Commentary insists the judge is the high priest, critiquing Calvin and Ainsworth for trying to split religious from civil jurisdiction. The Catholic reading sees an undivided theocratic authority vested in the high priest as God's vicegerent (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/deuteronomy-17.html). Ellicott (Anglican) sees a cooperative arrangement: priests as custodians of the Law, the judge as executor — a distinction preserved whether the judge is Joshua or a later king (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-17.html).

- **Kingship as permission vs. command:** Gill notes that Jewish tradition took v. 15 as a *command* ("thou shalt in any wise set him king over thee"), while most Protestant commentators read it as a *permission* anticipating Israel's future demand. The Targum of Jonathan prefaces the clause accordingly (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/17.htm). Dummelow underscores that kingship is "not disapproved" but the kingdom remains theocratic (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/deuteronomy-17.html).

- **Reformed emphasis on *lex rex*:** Ligonier highlights that this passage founds the constitutional principle that the law is above the king — rulers are subject to God's law no less than ordinary citizens. This became foundational in Western jurisprudence (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/king-and-law).

---

### Other Views

- **Catholic reading (Knox / New Advent):** The Knox translation renders v. 16 as a warning against foreign alliances with Egypt for cavalry, rather than a literal return to Egypt. The footnote explains: "What is here discouraged is not, probably, an attempt to invade Egypt, but an attempt to secure an alliance with Egypt which would enable Israel to put cavalry into the field" (https://www.newadvent.org/bible/deu017.htm).

- **Catholic Encyclopedia on "Deuteronomy":** The term means "copy" or "duplicate," not "second law." Pseudo-Athanasius maintained it signified "the second law," but the more common understanding is "explanation" or "exhortation" inducing observance of the law (https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/04761b.htm).

- **Septuagint interest:** Precept Austin notes the LXX translates *mishneh* ("copy") as *to deuteronomion*, which gave the entire book its English name — a mistranslation that stuck (https://www.preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-17-commentary). Ellicott confirms this (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-17.html).

- **Solomon as the test case:** Multiple commentators across traditions point to Solomon as the deliberate or self-deceived violator of vv. 16–17. Ellicott asks how Solomon could transgress — and answers that the same question could be asked of David moving the ark on a cart (2 Samuel 6). The law was known but the heart found ways to rationalize disobedience (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-17.html). Guzik adds that the human heart's capacity for self-justification ("how much is 'multiply'?") is the real culprit (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-17/).

- **The "evil" and the Lord's Prayer:** Ellicott notes that the Septuagint renders "the evil" in v. 7 as "the wicked man" (*ton poneron*), and this form is taken up by Paul in 1 Corinthians 5:13. This bears on the phrase "deliver us from evil" (*apo tou ponerou*) in the Lord's Prayer — "there is really no such thing as wickedness in the world apart from some wicked being or person" (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/deuteronomy-17.html).
